cards.explanation: The answer is that it is an abomination to the LORD. Moses says the first husband may not remarry her after she has been defiled, "…for that is an abomination to the LORD." Moses adds, "You must not bring sin upon the land that the LORD your God is giving you as an inheritance." So the reason comes from the LORD Himself, not from a vote.

The answer is that he stays home and brings joy to his wife. For one year he is free "…to stay at home and bring joy to the wife he has married." No war and no duty, just home and his bride. I think that's a pretty sweet deal, friends, and I'd sign up for a year of that in a heartbeat.

The answer is that it would take his livelihood as security. Moses says taking millstones "…would be taking one’s livelihood as security." The millstones are how he makes his daily bread. Imagine a lender walking off with my oven for a debt. I'd be sitting there with dough and a very sad face.

The answer is Miriam. Moses says, "Remember what the LORD your God did to Miriam on the journey after you came out of Egypt." He brings her up right after the instructions about skin diseases. Miriam was Moses' sister (Numbers 26:59), and her story is told in Numbers 12:10.

The answer is so he can sleep in his own cloak. Moses says to return it by sunset "…so that he may sleep in his own cloak and bless you…" For a poor man, the cloak was what he had to sleep in. Nobody should have to spend the night cold while his neighbor holds the blanket.

The answer is True. Moses says, "…this will be credited to you as righteousness before the LORD your God." That's said about returning the poor man's security by sunset, so that he may sleep in his own cloak. The LORD counts that as righteousness. A cloak handed back is a good return, friends.

The answer is False. The protection isn't only for Israelites. Moses says a poor and needy hired hand is covered "…whether he is a brother or a foreigner residing in one of your towns." Brother or foreigner, the rule is the same.

The answer is each day before sunset. Moses says, "You are to pay his wages each day before sunset…" Same day, no waiting. If I had to wait a week for my pay, I'd be eating crumbs off the counter by Wednesday.

The answer is that he depends on it to get by. Moses says to pay his wages each day before sunset, "…because he is poor and depends on them." So that pay isn't a small thing to him. Moses warns that if it's held back, the man may cry out to the LORD, and the one holding it back will be guilty of sin (Deuteronomy 24:15).

The answer is his own sin. Moses says, "each is to die for his own sin." Fathers aren't put to death for their children, and children aren't put to death for their fathers. Each person answers for his own.

The answer is that they were once slaves in Egypt. Moses says, "Remember that you were slaves in Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you from that place." Then he adds, "Therefore I am commanding you to do this." So the reason he gives is Israel's own story: slaves in Egypt, redeemed by the LORD. That's a whole lot of history packed into one "remember," friends.

The answer is bless. Moses says to leave the forgotten sheaf "…so that the LORD your God may bless you in all the work of your hands." The sheaf you leave behind goes to the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow. I'd call that a very good way to lose a sheaf, friends.

The answer is so their brother isn't degraded. Moses says no more than forty lashes, "…lest your brother be beaten any more than that and be degraded in your sight." Even a guilty man is still called your brother. The limit protects his dignity.

The answer is to muzzle it. Moses says, "Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain." The ox is working the grain, so it's not shut out from it. I'd say that's a fair deal for a hard worker, friends.

The answer is so his name isn't blotted out from Israel. Moses says the first son "…will carry on the name of the dead brother, so that his name will not be blotted out from Israel." The brother is gone, but his name keeps going through that son.

The answer is that he refuses to preserve his brother's name. She says, "My husband’s brother refuses to preserve his brother’s name in Israel. He is not willing to perform the duty of a brother-in-law for me." Notice she isn't dragging him off to a fight. She walks to the city gate and lays it out in front of the elders (Deuteronomy 25:7). And the elders don't just rule on the spot. They summon him and talk with him first (Deuteronomy 25:8).

The answer is that this is for the man who won't keep his brother's line. She declares, "This is what is done to the man who will not maintain his brother’s line." That's after the elders have spoken with him and he still says he doesn't want to marry her. It's a hard moment, friends.

The answer is so they may live long in the land. Moses says to keep accurate and honest weights and measures "…so that you may live long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you." Honest scales and a long life in the land go together in this verse, friends. A bag with one heavy weight and one light weight is exactly what he forbids (Deuteronomy 25:13). A scale that changes its mind depending on the customer is no scale at all.

The answer is True. Moses says, "For everyone who behaves dishonestly in regard to these things is detestable to the LORD your God." He means the weights and measures. A crooked scoop isn't a small thing to Him, friends.

The answer is the stragglers at the back. Moses says the Amalekites "…attacked all your stragglers…" Israel was "…tired and weary…" and the ones at the back got hit. I think that makes the story hard to hear, friends.

The answer is fear. Moses says of the Amalekites, "they had no fear of God." He recalls how they met Israel on the journey when the people were tired and weary, and attacked all the stragglers. That's what Moses names about them, friends.
